---
title: "Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model"
subtitle: "A spatio-temporal extension"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup-area-level
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "msoa_year_domain_frame.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(.data$area_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(.data$area_id)
```

```{r}
#| label: plotting-config
#| echo: false
share_label <- label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pp_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")
variance_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.0001)
missing_fill <- "grey85"
diverging_low <- "#2166ac"
diverging_high <- "#b2182b"

map_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  axis.title.y = element_text(
    size = 12,
    face = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    margin = margin(r = 15)
  ),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 9)
)

chart_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
)

map_annotation_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30")
)
```

Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previously. The Fay--Herriot model lets direct estimates for each area-time cell, an *MSOA-year cell* in this example, borrow strength from predictors and spatial and temporal structures to stabilise noisy estimates.

::: {.callout-note title="Theory in brief"}
The Fay--Herriot model treats each direct estimate as a noisy observation of the true area-time quantity:

$$
\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} = \mu_{jt} + e_{jt}, \qquad
e_{jt} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{jt}),
$$

where $\psi_{jt}$ is the sampling variance estimated from the survey design. The latent area-time mean is then modelled using predictors and an area random effect:

$$
\mu_{jt} = \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{jt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j.
$$

Here $u_j$ borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity $\mu_{jt}$. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect $v_t$ can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence.
:::

<div class="method-divider" aria-hidden="true"></div>

{{< include _includes/target-estimand.qmd >}}

## Prepare modelling data

First we join the complete area-time domain to the direct estimates and their sampling variances from the previous workbook, as well as the area predictors.

```{r}
#| label: load-direct-estimates
direct_estimates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "freq_walker_estimates_direct.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(-.data$msoa_name)

direct_walk <- domain_frame |>
  left_join(direct_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id"))

head(direct_walk)
```
```{r}
#| label: load-area-covariates
area_covariates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "area_covariates_daily_walking.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "area_id",
      "cov_population_density",
      "cov_share_no_car_households",
      "cov_share_work_from_home",
      "cov_share_students",
      "cov_share_routine_semiroutine"
    ))
  )
head(area_covariates)
```

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. `INLA` uses these indices to attach random effects to the correct area and period.

The FH specifications include two area-effect structures: an unstructured independent effect and a structured spatial effect. The spatial effect uses `area_inla_id` together with the adjacency graph. The independent effect uses a separate column, `area_iid_id` with the same indices so `INLA` treats the two area effects as separate model terms.

```{r}
#| label: define-model-index

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels),
  area_iid_id =seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)
```

To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph `.adj` as input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point. 

![](assets/spatial_weights_example.png)

```{r}
#| label: build-spatial-graph

msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(.data$area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)
```

The missing or zero sampling variances need to be handled before the modelling data are assembled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

- For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.
- Because the outcome is binary (`1` for walking daily, `0` otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of `0` when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-sampling-variance

max_variance <- max(
  direct_walk$variance[direct_walk$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

direct_walk_model <- direct_walk |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(.data$direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(.data$variance) ~ max_variance,
      .data$variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ .data$variance
    )
  )
```

Now, we assemble the modelling data for `INLA` by adding the area predictors and the numeric indices for the temporal and area effects.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-model-data

model_data <- direct_walk_model |>
  left_join(area_covariates, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  arrange(.data$time_id, .data$area_inla_id)

head(model_data)
```

## Fit and evaluate models

Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to `INLA` as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight.

We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using `INLA`. 

| Model | Name | Specifications |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Baseline | Intercept plus independent area effect |
| M1 | +Temporal | M0 plus temporal random walk |
| M2 | +Core predictors | M1 plus population density and no-car households |
| M3 | +All predictors | M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH) |
| M4 | +Spatial | M3 plus spatial structure among MSOA adjacency |

```{r}
#| label: fit-fh-models
#| code-fold: false

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)
```

:::{.callout-note}
When configuring `INLA` to fit an area-level FH model, these arguments are required:

- The `scale` argument passes the inverse sampling variance to `INLA`, so direct estimates with larger sampling variance contribute less to the likelihood. 
- The `control.family` block fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the observation-level uncertainty is already supplied by the direct estimate sampling variances.
:::

Next, we collate fitted values for all FH model specifications into one results table.

```{r}
#| label: collate-fh-results

# Main frame to keep from model data
output_cols <- c(
  "area_id",
  "time_id",
  "msoa_name",
  "direct_estimate",
  "variance",
  "n"
)

model_output_frame <- select(model_data, all_of(output_cols))

# Extract fitted values from each model and bind them to the frame
fh_result_tables <- map2(
  fh_fits,
  names(fh_fits),
  function(fit, model_name) {
    fitted_values <- as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)

    model_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values)

    transmute(
      model_results,
      model = model_name,
      across(all_of(output_cols)),
      fh_estimate = .data$mean,
      fh_variance = .data$sd^2,
      fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
      fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
      fh_ci_width = .data[["0.975quant"]] - .data[["0.025quant"]]
    )
  }
)

# Stack model outputs and set display order
fh_results <- bind_rows(fh_result_tables)
fh_results <- mutate(
  fh_results,
  model = factor(.data$model, levels = names(model_formulas)
)
)

head(fh_results)
```

To compare the fitted models' overall performance, we use `WAIC` or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by `INLA`; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

```{r}
#| label: waic-comparison
model_waic <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)

model_waic
```

M4 has the lowest WAIC and M0 is clearly the weakest model, suggesting that the temporal term, area predictors, and spatial structure together give the best overall fit among the FH specifications.

## Further diagnostics

### Direct To Baseline Model

We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, spatial structure, or temporal structure to understand how the FH models fundamentally handle noisy direct estimates. 

```{r}
#| label: prepare-direct-m0-comparison

fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per area-time cell, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m0 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]] - .data$variance
  )

wave_years <- sort(unique(fh_wide$time_id))
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-direct-m0-comparison
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 12
#| out-width: "100%"

variance_change_limit <- max(abs(direct_to_m0$variance_change), na.rm = TRUE) * .5
direct_variance_limit <- max(direct_to_m0$direct_variance, na.rm = TRUE)

direct_to_m0_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(direct_to_m0, by = "area_id")

plot_m0_variance_change <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m0_map_data |>
    filter(.data$time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$variance_change), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = diverging_low,
      mid = "white",
      high = diverging_high,
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-variance_change_limit, variance_change_limit),
      oob = squish,
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Change"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_direct_variance <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m0_map_data |>
    filter(.data$time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$direct_variance), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Reds",
      direction = 1,
      limits = c(0, direct_variance_limit),
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Variance"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

variance_change_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_m0_variance_change)
direct_variance_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_direct_variance)

variance_change_maps[[1]] <- variance_change_maps[[1]] +
  ylab("Variance change")
direct_variance_maps[[1]] <- direct_variance_maps[[1]] +
  ylab("Direct variance")

for (i in seq_len(length(wave_years) - 1)) {
  variance_change_maps[[i]] <- variance_change_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  direct_variance_maps[[i]] <- direct_variance_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

direct_to_m0_ranked <- direct_to_m0 |>
  filter(!is.na(variance_change)) |>
  group_by(time_id) |>
  # Rank within each wave by the original direct-estimate variance.
  arrange(direct_variance, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(variance_rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    time_id,
    variance_rank,
    `Variance change` = variance_change,
    `Variance (direct)` = direct_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(time_id, variance_rank),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  )

direct_to_m0_ranked_plot <- ggplot(
  direct_to_m0_ranked,
  aes(
    x = .data$variance_rank,
    y = .data$value,
    colour = .data$measure
  )
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$time_id), nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = variance_label) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Variance change" = "purple",
    "Variance (direct)" = "red"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "",
    x = "MSOAs sorted by variance",
    y = "Variance",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  chart_text_theme

(wrap_plots(c(variance_change_maps, direct_variance_maps), ncol = 3) /
  direct_to_m0_ranked_plot) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Direct estimates compared with baseline FH model (M0)",
    subtitle = "M0 stabilises noisy direct estimates before adding predictors or spatio-temporal structure",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```
Area-time cells with high sampling variance contain less reliable local information, so M0 pulls them more strongly toward its baseline prediction. The Bayesian FH fit also produces posterior estimates for cells with missing direct estimates or zero/missing variance, allowing sparse or unsampled area-time cells to remain in the output with explicit uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: missing-direct-m0-estimates
fh_wide |>
  filter(is.na(.data$direct_estimate) | is.na(.data$variance)) |>
  transmute(
    `MSOA` = .data$area_id,
    `Wave year` = .data$time_id,
    `Direct estimate` = share_label(.data$direct_estimate),
    `Sampling variance` = round(.data$variance, 6),
    `M0 estimate` = share_label(.data[["fh_estimate__M0 Baseline"]]),
    `M0 posterior variance` = round(
      .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]],
      6
    )
  )
```

### Adding Predictors

After the WAIC comparison, we inspect local estimate changes to see where the model moves the target estimates and whether those movements are substantively plausible. In Fay-Herriot SAE, adding predictors changes the expected value for each area-time cell, and unstable direct estimates are pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions when the predictors are relevant.

For example, moving from M2 to M3 adds the occupation and work-pattern predictors. We map where M3 changes the estimates relative to M2, then summarise the predictor profiles of the areas with the largest upward and downward shifts (top and bottom 10%).

```{r}
#| label: plot-m2-to-m3-change
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "100%"

m2_to_m3 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    estimate_change =
      .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]] - 
      .data[["fh_estimate__M2 +Core predictors"]]
  )

m2_to_m3_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = "area_id")

m2_to_m3_estimate_limit <- quantile(
  abs(m2_to_m3$estimate_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

plot_m2_to_m3_change <- function(wave) {
  m2_to_m3_map_data |>
    filter(.data$time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$estimate_change), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = diverging_low,
      mid = "white",
      high = diverging_high,
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-m2_to_m3_estimate_limit, m2_to_m3_estimate_limit),
      oob = squish,
      labels = pp_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Change"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

m2_to_m3_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_m2_to_m3_change)
m2_to_m3_maps[[1]] <- m2_to_m3_maps[[1]] + ylab("Estimate change")

for (i in seq_len(length(wave_years) - 1)) {
  m2_to_m3_maps[[i]] <- m2_to_m3_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

wrap_plots(m2_to_m3_maps, ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Estimate change after adding additional predictors",
    subtitle = "M3 minus M2",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```
```{r}
#| label: summarise-m2-to-m3-drivers
m2_to_m3_drivers <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    work_from_home = cov_share_work_from_home,
    students = cov_share_students,
    routine_semiroutine = cov_share_routine_semiroutine
  ) |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  mutate(
    change_group = case_when(
      estimate_change >= quantile(estimate_change, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Raised most by M3",
      estimate_change <= quantile(estimate_change, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Lowered most by M3",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

m2_to_m3_drivers |>
  filter(!is.na(.data$change_group)) |>
  group_by(.data$change_group) |>
  summarise(
    `Work from home` = mean(.data$work_from_home, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Students` = mean(.data$students, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Routine or semi-routine` = mean(.data$routine_semiroutine, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
The areas whose estimates are raised most by M3 have higher work-from-home and student shares, and lower routine/semi-routine occupation shares. This pattern is plausible: students and remote workers may have more flexible daily routines, shorter local trips, or lower car dependence, all of which could be associated with more walking for transport. The improvement in WAIC from M2 to M3 suggests that these added predictors also improve overall model fit.

### Adding Temporal And Spatial Effects

The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be examined through two diagnostic outputs by `INLA`:

- `tau` is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. A higher `tau` means the random effect varies less.
- `phi` is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A value of `0.5` means the structured and unstructured components contribute roughly equally to the area random effect.

```{r}
#| label: tau-phi

fh_fits[["M4 +Spatial"]]$summary.hyperpar |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |>
  filter(str_detect(.data$parameter, "time_inla_id|area_inla_id|Phi")) |>
  select(parameter, mean, sd, `0.025quant`, `0.5quant`, `0.975quant`) |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
  )
```

The temporal effect has a high `tau` than the spatial effect, indicating smaller differences between survey waves than between MSOAs. Meanwhile, the low spatial `phi` (less than `0.5`) indicates that only a small share of the remaining between-area variation follows the spatial weights; most of it remains unstructured. 

We can see where that structured spatial component affects the estimates by mapping the change from M3 to M4. In most areas the changes are small, with some clustered adjustments where neighbouring MSOAs share similar estimated walking rates, such as the more urban southern region.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-change-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "100%"
m3_to_m4 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    estimate_change =
      .data[["fh_estimate__M4 +Spatial"]] -
      .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]]
  )

m3_to_m4_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(m3_to_m4, by = "area_id")

m3_to_m4_limit <- quantile(
  abs(m3_to_m4$estimate_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

plot_m3_to_m4_change <- function(wave) {
  m3_to_m4_map_data |>
    filter(.data$time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$estimate_change), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = diverging_low,
      mid = "white",
      high = diverging_high,
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-m3_to_m4_limit, m3_to_m4_limit),
      oob = squish,
      labels = pp_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Change"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

m3_to_m4_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_m3_to_m4_change)
m3_to_m4_maps[[1]] <- m3_to_m4_maps[[1]] + ylab("Estimate change")

for (i in seq_len(length(wave_years) - 1)) {
  m3_to_m4_maps[[i]] <- m3_to_m4_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

wrap_plots(m3_to_m4_maps, ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Estimate change after adding spatial smoothing",
    subtitle = "M4 minus M3",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```


## Report estimates and uncertainty

Choosing the final model requires performance diagnostics, domain knowledge about the estimand, and enough metadata for downstream interpretation. Further benchmarking, such as comparison with related external indicators or sensitivity checks, can strengthen this decision when suitable data are available.

The final model estimates should be reported with their associated uncertainty. In the maps below, uncertainty is shown as the width of the posterior 95% credible interval. For transparency, the output should also retain the direct estimates, sample sizes, and direct-estimate variances.

```{r}
#| label: select-final-fh-model
# Keep only the final, most structured model.
final_fh_results <- fh_results |>
  filter(.data$model == "M4 +Spatial") |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    n,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance,
    fh_lower,
    fh_upper,
    fh_ci_width
  )

head(final_fh_results)
```

```{r}
#| label: final-model-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 12
#| out-width: "100%"

final_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(final_fh_results, by = "area_id")
final_estimate_limits <- range(final_fh_results$fh_estimate, na.rm = TRUE)
final_ci_width_limits <- c(0, max(final_fh_results$fh_ci_width, na.rm = TRUE))
final_wave_years <- sort(unique(final_fh_results$time_id))

plot_final_estimate <- function(wave) {
  final_map_data |>
    filter(.data$time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$fh_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "magma",
      limits = final_estimate_limits,
      labels = share_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Share"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_final_ci_width <- function(wave) {
  final_map_data |>
    filter(.data$time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$fh_ci_width), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Oranges",
      direction = 1,
      limits = final_ci_width_limits,
      labels = pp_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "95% CI width"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

estimate_maps <- lapply(final_wave_years, plot_final_estimate)
uncertainty_maps <- lapply(final_wave_years, plot_final_ci_width)

estimate_maps[[1]] <- estimate_maps[[1]] + ylab("Final estimate")
uncertainty_maps[[1]] <- uncertainty_maps[[1]] + ylab("95% CI width")

for (i in seq_len(length(final_wave_years) - 1)) {
  estimate_maps[[i]] <- estimate_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  uncertainty_maps[[i]] <- uncertainty_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

wrap_plots(c(estimate_maps, uncertainty_maps), ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Share of adults who walk for transport daily",
    subtitle = "Spatio-temporal FH model (M4), 95% CI width",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```

Even after the direct estimates have been stabilised through the Fay-Herriot model, weaker survey coverage can still leave year-specific patterns in the modelled estimates. The generally higher 2023 estimates are consistent with weaker survey coverage in that wave, so the modelled estimates should be read alongside posterior interval widths and original sample sizes.

```{r}
#| label: export-fh-results
#| echo: false
write_csv(
  final_fh_results,
  file.path(base_path, "freq_walker_estimates_area-fh.csv")
)
```
